topicName: Globalisation and the New World Order
description: A study of globalisation as the growing interconnection of the world's economies, societies and cultures, the post-Cold War new world order, the forces driving global integration, and the mixed effects of these processes on Africa and Tanzania.

options.text: The division of the world into rival military blocs
The increasing interconnection of the world's economies, societies and cultures
The withdrawal of nations from international trade
The forced colonisation of African states by Europe

mcq.explanation: Globalisation refers to the process by which the world's economies, societies and cultures become increasingly interconnected and interdependent through trade, technology and communication.

mcq.questionText: The term 'new world order' is most closely associated with the period after which event?

options.text: The end of the Cold War

mcq.explanation: The 'new world order' describes the global arrangement after the Cold War ended around 1991, marked by a largely unipolar world led by the USA and the spread of liberal democracy and the free market.

mcq.questionText: After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the new world order was described as 'unipolar' because:

options.text: Two superpowers continued to dominate equally
The United States emerged as the single dominant superpower
Africa became the centre of world politics
China replaced the USA as the leading power

mcq.explanation: With the USSR gone, the USA stood as the only remaining superpower, making the world unipolar and dominated by a single centre of power.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a major economic driving force of globalisation?

options.text: The growth of multinational and transnational corporations

mcq.explanation: Multinational and transnational corporations operate across many countries, spreading capital, goods and production worldwide, and are a key engine of globalisation.

mcq.questionText: Which international institution chiefly regulates trade rules among member countries?
mcq.explanation: The WTO, established in 1995, sets and enforces the rules of international trade among its member states.

mcq.questionText: The IMF and the World Bank were both created at which 1944 conference?
mcq.explanation: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were established at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 to manage the post-war global economy.

mcq.questionText: Which technological development has most accelerated globalisation in recent decades?

options.text: The internet and information and communication technology (ICT)

mcq.explanation: The internet and ICT allow instant communication, information sharing and trade across the globe, greatly speeding up globalisation.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a positive effect of globalisation?

options.text: Transfer of technology and skills between countries
The widening gap between rich and poor nations

mcq.explanation: Globalisation can transfer technology, skills and knowledge from developed to developing countries, which is one of its benefits.

mcq.questionText: Critics argue that globalisation promotes 'neo-colonialism' because:

options.text: It restores direct colonial administration over Africa
Powerful nations and corporations control weaker economies indirectly through trade and finance
It removes all foreign influence from developing countries
It guarantees equal wealth for all nations

mcq.explanation: Neo-colonialism describes how rich countries and multinationals dominate poorer ones through economic means such as loans, trade terms and investment, rather than direct rule.

mcq.questionText: The movement of skilled professionals such as doctors from developing countries to wealthier nations is called:
mcq.explanation: Brain drain is the loss of skilled and educated people who migrate to richer countries for better opportunities, weakening the development of their home countries.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following best illustrates cultural globalisation in Tanzania?

options.text: The disappearance of all foreign goods from markets
The spread of foreign music, films, fashion and fast food alongside local culture
A complete ban on the internet
The end of all international trade agreements

mcq.explanation: Cultural globalisation is seen in the spread of foreign music, films, fashion and food, which mix with and sometimes threaten local cultures.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a common criticism that globalisation harms developing economies?

options.text: It makes them produce too many manufactured goods
It deepens their dependency on developed countries for capital, technology and markets
It forces them to stop exporting

mcq.explanation: A central criticism is that globalisation keeps developing countries dependent on rich nations for capital, technology and markets, limiting their independent growth.

mcq.questionText: How can African countries like Tanzania best benefit from globalisation?

options.text: By isolating themselves completely from the world economy
By investing in education, technology and value-added production to compete globally
By exporting only unprocessed raw materials forever

mcq.explanation: By improving education, adopting technology and adding value to their products, African countries can compete and gain more from global markets rather than being exploited.

mcq.questionText: Regional economic groupings such as the East African Community (EAC) and SADC are an African response to globalisation because they:

options.text: Withdraw Africa from world trade entirely
Strengthen cooperation and bargaining power among member states

mcq.explanation: Regional blocs help African states pool resources, expand markets and negotiate collectively, improving their position in a globalised world.

mcq.questionText: Which factor, besides trade and technology, has been important in promoting globalisation?

options.text: Improvements in transport such as containers, ships and air travel
The decline of all communication systems
The reduction of world population to a single country

mcq.explanation: Faster and cheaper transport, including containerisation, shipping and air travel, has made it easier to move goods and people, driving globalisation.

fib.questionText: Globalisation is the increasing _____ of the world's economies, societies and cultures.
fib.explanation: Globalisation centres on the growing interconnection and interdependence of the world.

fib.questionText: The new world order emerged after the end of the _____ War around 1991.
fib.explanation: The new world order followed the end of the Cold War and the collapse of the Soviet Union.

fib.questionText: After the Cold War the world became largely _____, dominated by a single superpower, the USA.
fib.explanation: A unipolar world is dominated by one centre of power, in this case the United States.

fib.questionText: The _____ Trade Organisation (WTO) regulates the rules of international trade among its members.
fib.explanation: The World Trade Organisation, founded in 1995, oversees global trade rules.

fib.questionText: The IMF and the World Bank were created in 1944 at the _____ Woods Conference.
fib.explanation: The Bretton Woods Conference established the IMF and the World Bank.

fib.questionText: Companies that operate in many countries at once are called _____ corporations.
fib.explanation: Multinational (or transnational) corporations operate across several countries and drive globalisation.

fib.questionText: The loss of skilled professionals who migrate to wealthier countries is known as _____ drain.
fib.explanation: Brain drain weakens developing countries by removing their educated and skilled workers.

fib.questionText: The indirect economic domination of poorer nations by powerful states and corporations is called _____.
fib.explanation: Neo-colonialism is control exercised through economic means rather than direct colonial rule.

fib.questionText: The fast worldwide sharing of information through the _____ has greatly accelerated globalisation.
fib.explanation: The internet and ICT enable instant global communication and trade.

fib.questionText: In the new world order, the economic system widely promoted was the free _____ economy.
fib.explanation: The free market economy, alongside liberal democracy, spread widely after the Cold War.

tf.questionText: Globalisation refers to the increasing interconnection of the world's economies, societies and cultures.
tf.explanation: This is the standard definition of globalisation.

tf.questionText: The new world order describes the global situation after the end of the Cold War.
tf.explanation: The new world order is the post-Cold War arrangement led largely by the USA.

tf.questionText: After the Cold War the world became bipolar, with two equal superpowers.
tf.explanation: The world became unipolar, dominated by the USA, after the USSR collapsed; bipolarity existed during the Cold War.

tf.questionText: The World Trade Organisation was established to regulate international trade among member states.
tf.explanation: The WTO, founded in 1995, oversees the rules of world trade.

tf.questionText: The IMF and World Bank were created at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85.
tf.explanation: They were created at the Bretton Woods Conference of 1944; the Berlin Conference dealt with the partition of Africa.

tf.questionText: Technology and the internet are among the main driving forces of globalisation.
tf.explanation: ICT and the internet are key forces speeding up global integration.

tf.questionText: Globalisation has only positive effects and no negative consequences.
tf.explanation: Globalisation also brings negatives such as inequality, dependency, exploitation, cultural erosion and environmental harm.

tf.questionText: Brain drain refers to the migration of skilled people from developing to developed countries.
tf.explanation: Brain drain is the loss of skilled professionals to wealthier nations.

tf.questionText: Globalisation can transfer technology and skills from developed to developing countries.
tf.explanation: Technology transfer is one of the recognised benefits of globalisation.

tf.questionText: Critics argue that globalisation widens inequality and deepens dependency for poor nations.
tf.explanation: A major criticism is that globalisation increases the gap between rich and poor and keeps weaker economies dependent.

summary.correctAnswer: Globalisation is the process by which the world's economies, societies and cultures become increasingly interconnected and interdependent through trade, technology, communication and the movement of people.
summary.explanation: This captures the economic, social and cultural dimensions of growing global integration.

summary.questionText: What is meant by the 'new world order' after the Cold War?
summary.correctAnswer: The new world order is the global arrangement after the Cold War, characterised by a largely unipolar world led by the USA, together with the spread of liberal democracy and the free market economy.
summary.explanation: It describes US dominance and the global spread of Western political and economic models after 1991.

summary.questionText: Mention four driving forces of globalisation.
summary.correctAnswer: Trade; multinational and transnational corporations; technology and the internet/ICT; improved transport; and international institutions such as the WTO, IMF and World Bank.
summary.explanation: These forces move goods, capital, information and people rapidly across the world.

summary.questionText: Name the three main international economic institutions linked to globalisation.
summary.correctAnswer: The World Trade Organisation (WTO), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
summary.explanation: These institutions shape global trade, finance and development policy.

summary.questionText: State four positive effects of globalisation.
summary.correctAnswer: Expansion of trade; transfer of technology and skills; easier access to information; increased foreign investment; and cultural exchange between peoples.
summary.explanation: These are the commonly recognised benefits of greater global integration.

summary.questionText: State four negative effects or criticisms of globalisation.
summary.correctAnswer: Widening inequality; dependency and neo-colonialism; exploitation of labour and resources; cultural erosion; brain drain; and environmental harm.
summary.explanation: Critics highlight these costs, especially for developing countries.

summary.questionText: Explain how globalisation has affected Africa and Tanzania.
summary.correctAnswer: It has brought investment, technology, markets and information, but also exposed Africa to unfair trade terms, dependency, exploitation of raw materials, cultural erosion and brain drain, often keeping the continent in a weaker economic position.
summary.explanation: Africa experiences both opportunities and serious challenges from globalisation.

summary.questionText: What is neo-colonialism in the context of globalisation?
summary.correctAnswer: Neo-colonialism is the indirect domination of weaker, formerly colonised nations by powerful states and corporations through economic means such as trade terms, loans, aid conditions and investment, rather than direct political rule.
summary.explanation: It explains how economic control replaces formal colonialism in a globalised world.

summary.questionText: Suggest ways African countries can benefit more from globalisation.
summary.correctAnswer: By investing in education and skills, adopting and developing technology, adding value to raw materials, strengthening regional groupings like the EAC and SADC, improving good governance, and negotiating fair trade terms.
summary.explanation: These measures help Africa compete and reduce exploitation in the global economy.

summary.questionText: Why is technology considered central to globalisation?
summary.correctAnswer: Technology, especially the internet and ICT together with modern transport, allows instant communication, rapid movement of goods, money and information, and links businesses and people across the world, making global integration possible and faster.
summary.explanation: Without modern technology the speed and scale of globalisation would not be possible.

hoq.questionText: A Tanzanian factory closes because cheap imported manufactured goods flood the local market, while the country continues to export mainly unprocessed minerals and crops. This situation best illustrates which criticism of globalisation?

options.text: That globalisation guarantees equal development for all nations
That globalisation can deepen dependency and disadvantage weaker economies through unequal trade
That globalisation always strengthens local industries
That globalisation ends all foreign investment

hoq.explanation: Exporting raw materials while importing finished goods and losing local industry reflects how unequal trade under globalisation can deepen dependency and harm developing economies.

hoq.questionText: Two countries join a regional bloc, lower trade barriers between themselves, and negotiate jointly with powerful trading partners. Why is this a sensible strategy in the globalised new world order?

options.text: Because isolation from world trade is the only path to growth
Because larger combined markets and collective bargaining improve their competitiveness and negotiating power
Because regional blocs abolish the need for any technology
Because it forces other countries to stop trading globally

hoq.explanation: Regional integration creates bigger markets and stronger collective bargaining, helping small economies cope with and benefit from globalisation rather than facing powerful partners alone.

hoq.questionText: Some historians argue that the post-Cold War spread of liberal democracy and the free market was not purely neutral progress. Which interpretation best supports a balanced, critical view?

options.text: The new world order benefited every country equally with no drawbacks
While it expanded markets and freedoms, it also reinforced the dominance of powerful states and corporations, sometimes at the expense of weaker nations
It had no effect on developing countries at all
It immediately ended global inequality and exploitation

hoq.explanation: A balanced view recognises both the opportunities of the new world order and how it strengthened existing global power imbalances, reflecting accurate historical analysis.
